newsitem.title: USA: Grandmother recalls painful Oklahoma bombing photo.
newsitem.headline: Grandmother recalls painful Oklahoma bombing photo.

text.p: A grandmother being questioned as a prospective juror said Wednesday her most enduring memory of the Oklahoma City bombing was the picture of a fireman carrying a small child out of the wreckage.

The woman, who worked in the circulation department at a newspaper in a small Colorado town, was the 74th prospective juror to be questioned about a range of subjects including their memories of the event and views on the death penalty.

"If someone has done a terrible crime perhaps they should be punished in a like manner," said the woman, who said she has been married more than 50 years and plays clarinet in her community band. But she added she was not confident that she should be the person to vote for execution if accused bomber Timothy McVeigh is found guilty.

The Gulf War veteran was charged with bombing the Alfred P. Murrah federal building in Oklahoma City on April 19, 1995, killing 168 people, including 19 children. He pleaded not guilty and faces the death penalty if convicted.

Security remained tight as the second anniversary of the bombing approached. Some 70 miles (110 kms) south of Denver, NORAD and the U.S. Space Command announced that all public tours at their headquarters were cancelled until further notice.

Barricades were placed outside the headquarters because of "possible security concerns," a spokeswoman said on Wednesday. She declined to say the security was specifically related to the April 19 anniversaries of the Oklahoma City bombing and the 1993 siege at Waco, Texas, where about 80 members of the Branch Davidian sect died in a standoff with federal agents.

In addition to remembering the photograph of a firefighter carrying the limp body of a young bombing victim, the potential juror said she remembered the nursery, referring to the day care centre at the Murrah building.

Two other prospective jurors were also questioned, bringing the total at midday to 76. The jurors were not told if they would be selected to serve on the trial, which is likely to last several months.
Their identity was kept secret and they were referred to in court only by a number. They sat behind a wooden screen out of the view of most of the spectators in the courtroom.
Jury selection is expected to be completed by next week.
